title: $47,000 a Year Is How Much an Hour? (2026)
metaDescription: $47,000 a year is $22.60/hour at 40 hrs/week — $903.85 weekly, $3,917 monthly. Full 2026 breakdown with a federal take-home estimate.

hero.lede: Based on a 40-hour week worked 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). Below: every pay-period equivalent, the rate at other workweeks, a 2026 federal take-home estimate, and how $47,000 compares with the U.S. median.

shortAnswer.heading: How much is $47,000 a year per hour?
shortAnswer.html: $47,000 a year is $22.60 an hour at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). That's $180.77 a day, $903.85 a week, $1,807.69 biweekly, and $3,916.67 a month — all gross. After estimated federal income tax and FICA, a single filer keeps about $39,945 a year, roughly $3,329 a month.

sections.title: What $47,000 looks like per paycheck.
sections.note: All figures are gross (pre-tax). See the take-home table below for the federal-only estimate after taxes.

sections.title: Where $47,000 stands in 2026.
paragraphs: At 40 hours a week, $47,000 a year is $22.60 an hour. That is the offer-letter number, not the bank-deposit number: gross pay lands at $1,807.69 per biweekly check, and what actually arrives depends on taxes and benefits withheld.

For scale, the median full-time U.S. worker earns $1,251 weekly per the BLS (BLS, Q2 2026), roughly $65,052 a year, so this salary is about 28% under the midpoint. A useful rule of thumb at this level: every extra $1 of hourly pay is worth about $2,080 a year at full time, so small raises compound faster than they feel.

sections.title: The hourly rate depends on your hours.
sections.note: Salaried roles rarely pay overtime — at 45 hours a week the same $47,000 effectively pays $20.09 per hour worked.

sections.title: From $47,000 gross to take-home.
sections.note: Single filer, standard deduction, no state/local income tax, no credits or pre-tax benefits. Your actual paycheck will differ.

sections.title: Why the 12% bracket doesn't mean 12% tax.
paragraphs: Only $30,900 of this salary is actually taxable federally once the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 is applied. Federal income tax totals $3,460 — a 7.4% effective rate even though the marginal bracket is 12% — and employee FICA adds $3,596.

After those federal deductions, take-home is roughly $39,945 a year — $1,536.33 per biweekly paycheck. On a 50/30/20 plan that budget supports about $1,664/month of essentials, $999/month of discretionary spending, and $666/month toward savings, before any state income tax.

faq.q: How much is $47,000 a year per hour?
faq.a: $47,000 a year is $22.60 an hour at 40 hours a week (2,080 hours a year). At 37.5 hours a week it rises to $24.10 an hour, and if you actually work 45-hour weeks it averages $20.09 per hour worked.

faq.q: How much is $47,000 a year biweekly?
faq.a: Gross biweekly pay on $47,000 is $1,807.69 ($47,000 ÷ 26 pay periods). After estimated federal income tax and FICA for a single filer, roughly $1,536.33 per check remains — before state taxes and benefits.

faq.q: How much is $47,000 a year after taxes?
faq.a: Using 2026 federal brackets and the $16,100 standard deduction, a single filer earning $47,000 pays about $3,460 in federal income tax and $3,596 in FICA, keeping roughly $39,945 a year ($3,328.71 a month). This is a federal-only estimate — state and local taxes reduce it further.

$47,000 is about 28% below the U.S. median full-time salary of roughly $65,052 (BLS, Q2 2026: $1,251/week). Whether it is "good" depends heavily on your metro's cost of living, household size, and debt load — the same salary goes much further in a low-cost region than in an expensive coastal city.

faq.q: What tax bracket is $47,000 in for 2026?
faq.a: After the $16,100 standard deduction, $47,000 leaves $30,900 of taxable income, which puts a single filer in the 12% marginal bracket for 2026. Only income above each threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so the effective federal rate is just 7.4%.

methodology: Conversions are straight arithmetic on gross salary: $47,000 ÷ 2,080 hours (40 × 52) for hourly, ÷ 260 workdays for daily, ÷ 52, 26, 24 and 12 for the pay-period figures. No taxes are applied to those rows.

The take-home estimate uses 2026 federal brackets for a single filer with the $16,100 standard deduction, plus employee FICA (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare). It excludes state/local income tax, credits, and pre-tax benefits such as 401(k) or health premiums — so real paychecks will differ.
The median comparison uses BLS median usual weekly earnings for full-time wage and salary workers: $1,251/week (BLS, Q2 2026).
Educational estimates only — not tax, legal, or financial advice.
